document.title: Post-Conference Comments of Illinois Municipal Electric Agency re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
) 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
) 
) 
 
POST-CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF ILLINOIS MUNICIPAL ELECTRIC AGENCY 
 
Illinois Municipal Electric Agency (“IMEA”) respectfully submits these comments in 
response to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC’s”) Notice Requesting Post-
Conference Comment (“Notice”).1  IMEA is an intervenor in the instant proceeding.2 
IMEA is a municipal joint action agency organized under Illinois law as a municipal 
corporation and unit of local government of the State of Illinois.3  IMEA is comprised of thirty-
two municipal members, all of which own and operate their own municipal electric systems in the 
State of Illinois and provide electricity to their end-use customers.  IMEA load is split roughly 
evenly between PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) and Midcontinent Independent System 
Operator, Inc.  IMEA provides a fully bundled and delivered, full-requirements service to each of 
its members and as such is the Load Serving Entity responsible for meeting certain obligations 
imposed by the Regional Transmission Organizations (“RTOs”) such as PJM. 
IMEA is a member of PJM’s  Electric Distributor sector.  In an effort to best facilitate 
reforms to PJM’s governance structure and stakeholder processes as a member thereof, IMEA 
submits answers to the questions found in the Appendix to the Commission’s Notice,4 and provides 
clarifying comments in each applicable question below. 
 
 
 
1 Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment, Docket No. AD26-7-000 (July 30, 2026). 
2 (doc-less) Motion to Intervene of Illinois Municipal Electric Agency under AD26-7-000 (August 21, 2026). 
3 65 ILCS 5/11-119.1-1 et seq. (2026). 
4 Notice at 3-6.

2 
 
I. 
PJM BOARD OF INDEPENDENCE 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
1) 
Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
X 
 
Comments: Three years is too short, but five or more years is too long.  Four is 
appropriate. 
2) 
Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board member may 
serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
X 
 
 
Comments: A Board member should serve, as long as they are elected by stakeholders, no 
longer than two terms of four years each (i.e., maximum of eight years of service). 
3) 
Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide a 
preference for some Board members that reside in the PJM region? 
X 
 
Comments: It is not necessary that a Board member reside in the PJM region, although 
maintaining a residence in the PJM region may be prudent.  In-person attendance at 
meetings with an in-person option should be encouraged. 
4) 
Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the cooling off 
period for Board members from two years to one year? 
X 
 
 
Comments: So long as the restrictions on financial interests are maintained or 
strengthened, a one-year cool off period is sufficient and would aid in expanding the 
candidate pool. 
5) 
Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable more 
communication between the Board and stakeholders? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Yes, Board communication with stakeholders is essential. 
6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made public or 
the Board be required to explain its reasoning? 
X 
 
 
Comments: The Board should be required to explain its reasoning, especially in the 
instances in which it proceeds with a proposal that differs in substance from what passes 
through the stakeholder process. 
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be open or 
available to the public? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Though Board Decisional Letters are a useful tool in understanding the Board’s 
thought process, these come only after the decision has been made.  Opening some Board 
meetings to the public would increase transparency and strengthen communication. 
8) 
Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state that the 
responsibility of PJM and its Board is to serve the public interest? 
 
X 
 
Comments: PJM’s primary purpose is to maintain reliability through its markets and 
planning processes.  Expanding its scope only risks further complicating its current outlook 
at a time when operations need to be streamlined.

3 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
9) 
Should state representatives have at least one voting member on the 
Nominating Committee? 
 
X 
 
Comments: PJM covers a large service territory comprised of states each with their own 
resource adequacy, transmission, and energy outlooks.  The inclusion of a state 
representative on the Nominating Committee risks politicizing a process which needs to be 
geared towards PJM’s north star – maintaining reliability.  That would be more difficult if a 
process already as challenging as finding qualified Board members was made more so by 
expanding the criteria for inclusion on the Nominating Committee.   
10) Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and tie management 
compensation to their achievement? 
 
X 
 
Comments: Public performance metrics tied to compensation can lead to compensation-
oriented thinking in a way that sacrifices quality of work product.  For example, if “Target 
A” is tied to compensation, an organization may priority “Target A” at the expense of other 
meaningful “Targets” which are not tied to compensation.  PJM should work with 
stakeholders and the Board to prioritize a work plan, and all parties involved should stick 
to it. 
 
II. 
SECTION 205 FILING RIGHTS 
 
 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
11) 
Should the stakeholder process be advisory, i.e., stakeholder votes only 
inform the Board? 
 
X 
 
Comments: As an electric distributor and load serving entity which participates in an RTO 
with an advisory stakeholder process, MISO, IMEA strongly disagrees with the idea of 
making the PJM stakeholder process advisory.  The tasks that PJM is faced with on a 
daily basis – keeping the lights on for the 67,000,000 Americans within its service 
territory – is enormous.  As the bulk electric system becomes more complex, that job only 
becomes more difficult.  The stakeholder process in PJM offers enormous benefit through 
the communication and collaboration it enables by allowing both PJM and stakeholders to 
thoughtfully work through issues that are too demanding, too important, and too complex 
to be solved by any one party individually.  While it is clear that reforms to the 
stakeholder process are necessary for the sake of efficiency, these changes can be found 
within the process itself, not the rights held by stakeholders.  A purely advisory process 
would erode the checks and balances which exist today and greatly diminish the ability 
for stakeholders to contribute to the decisions which will ultimately affect their interests, 
and the downstream effect would be lessened transparency, trust, and balance in PJM’s 
day-to-day proceedings.

4 
 
 
III. 
STAKEHOLDER PROCESS 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
16) Should the approval threshold in the Members Committee be lowered from 
two-thirds sector-weighted voting? 
X 
 
 
Comments: Interests are too diverse today to expect a two-thirds majority with the 
frequency necessary to move important items along.  For that reason, yes, the approval 
threshold in the Members Committee should be lowered to a simple majority. 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
12) Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over the energy market and 
ancillary services unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of 
two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
 
X 
 
Comments: The two-thirds majority is a threshold which promotes consensus building 
amongst stakeholders and ultimately results in proposals which have been subjected to 
increased scrutiny for the betterment of the RTO as a whole.  Nonetheless, two-thirds is a 
demanding statute in today’s environment and lowering it to a simple majority would foster 
efficiency gains without sacrificing needed rigor.  Further, PJM already has 205 filing 
rights over the energy and ancillary services market, which are not the subject of current 
reforms.  Current reform efforts are aimed at the capacity market. 
13) Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over Regional Transmission 
Expansion Planning (RTEP) unencumbered by the requirement to obtain 
approval of two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
 
X 
 
Comments: Just as with the energy and ancillary service markets, the need to obtain a two-
thirds supermajority is a requirement which promotes collaboration amongst stakeholders 
and PJM.  With that said, two-thirds is a high mark, and lowering it to a simple majority 
would promote collaboration while facilitating greater efficiency. 
14) Should the Organization of PJM States Inc (OPSI) have “jump ball” rights 
over resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation filings when a 
supermajority of OPSI agrees on an alternative proposal? 
 
X 
 
Comments: While OPSI should have an augmented role in PJM’s stakeholder process, it 
should not have “jump ball” rights over resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation 
filings, given the outsized influence this would provide, which would diminish the need for 
collaboration. 
15) Should the Members Committee have “jump ball” filing rights over the 
portions of the tariff where PJM has 205 filing rights when a supermajority 
of stakeholders approves an alternative proposal? 
X 
 
 
Comments: The need for this can be best illustrated using PJM’s recent Reliability 
Backstop Auction filing (ER26-3380).  PJM’s filing did not incorporate many of the key 
elements that were approved by stakeholders.  The ability for a supermajority of 
stakeholders to have “jump ball” filing rights would allow for the Commission to consider 
a more fulsome panorama of opinions, at no detriment to the Commission.

5 
 
17) Should the voting rules barring affiliate votes, which apply to senior 
standing committees, also apply to lower-level committees? 
 
X 
 
Comments: This would be a simple solution to allow for affiliate members to have an 
increased voice in the stakeholder process. 
 
STATE PARTICIPATION 
 
 
Questions/Comments 
Yes No 
18) In addition to OPSI, should there be a second state representative group 
consisting of governors’ representatives and/or state legislators’ 
representatives? 
 
X 
 
Comments: The states have funding and representation through the Organization of PJM 
States, Inc. (OPSI).  If PJM wishes to emulate the method of state participation in MISO, it 
might consider augmenting the role of OPSI to mirror that of the Organization of MISO 
States (OMS), in lieu of splintering and diluting the states' voice through the creation of 
another new stakeholder group.  OMS is highly regarded and operates in conjunction with 
MISO, the MISO Board, and stakeholders, on many issues.  It is important for states to 
have their voices heard, but a second state organization may actually have the unintended 
consequences of complicating the conversation and adding to the confusion.  PJM needs to 
be streamlining its process to make it more efficient if it wants to be more effective.  A 
second entity could have the opposite effect, and in fact, PJM already has the tools today to 
bolster the states through OPSI.  Doing so would not necessitate the creation of a new 
stakeholder body nor the funding thereto.  Additionally, as PJM stated at the Technical 
Conference, within the same state PJM tends to hear differing viewpoints on the same 
issue. Maintaining OPSI as the states' vector of communication and participation, perhaps 
in an enhanced role, would solidify and amplify the state's voice through the usage of an 
already existing, funded, and respected entity.  An augmented OPSI could, for example, be 
adjusted to reflect a broader group of government/state representatives. 
19) Should state representatives have a formal voting role in the stakeholder 
process (limited to certain topics, such as resource adequacy and regional 
transmission cost allocation) in addition to the consumer advocate votes? 
 
X 
 
Comments: State jurisdiction lies at the retail, not wholesale level.  Communication 
between states and PJM, as exists with OPSI, is important.  But voting rights on FERC-
jurisdictional issues would be inappropriate. 
20) Should PJM be required to consult with OPSI prior to making a section 205 
filing related to resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation? 
X 
 
 
Comments: In light of diversifying needs across the region, consultation with OPSI is a 
requirement that would give both PJM and OPSI a beneficial opportunity for 
communication.

6 
 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
 
WHEREFORE, for the reasons set forth herein, IMEA does hereby submit the instant 
comments pursuant to the Commission’s Notice. 
 
 
Respectfully Submitted,
